clinicalPearls: A rare, severe form of cutaneous mastocytosis of infancy with diffuse mast cell infiltration of the whole skin
The skin is thickened with a doughy or leathery texture rather than discrete lesions
Extensive blistering and erythroderma can occur, and the large mast cell burden risks severe mediator release
Massive histamine release can cause flushing, hypotension and life-threatening reactions, sometimes triggered by handling or medications
Baseline tryptase is often markedly elevated reflecting the high mast cell load
Careful trigger avoidance, anaphylaxis preparedness and mediator-targeted therapy are essential
reference.pathophysiology: In diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis, clonal mast cells infiltrate the entire dermis rather than forming discrete lesions, giving generalised skin thickening. The very large cutaneous mast cell burden means that degranulation, provoked by mechanical trauma, temperature change, drugs or infection, can release enough mediator to cause extensive blistering and dangerous systemic effects including hypotension and shock. The high mast cell mass is reflected in a markedly raised tryptase, and affected infants are vulnerable to severe, potentially fatal mediator crises.
additionalDifferentials: Epidermolysis bullosa or other blistering disorders of infancy
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing dense diffuse dermal mast cell infiltration
Identification of triggers and a documented anaphylaxis plan
Monitoring for complications during illness or procedures
redFlags: Hypotension, extensive blistering or shock from mediator release
Severe reactions triggered by handling, drugs or infection
Very high tryptase with systemic symptoms
Failure to thrive or systemic involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition can improve over childhood, but the infantile course may be complicated by dangerous mediator crises; with careful management and avoidance of triggers, many children improve with age.
pitfalls: Underestimating the risk of catastrophic mediator release
Using known mast cell-degranulating drugs without caution
Confusing extensive blistering with a primary bullous disease
Failing to equip carers with an anaphylaxis plan
management: Institute strict avoidance of mast cell degranulation triggers such as mechanical friction, temperature change and culprit drugs including opioids and NSAIDs
Control mediator symptoms with H1 and H2 antihistamines and mast cell stabilisers such as sodium cromoglicate
Provide adrenaline auto-injectors and a documented anaphylaxis action plan given the risk of life-threatening mediator crises
Treat acute mediator crises and hypotension urgently with adrenaline, antihistamines and fluid resuscitation
Give meticulous skin care and manage blistering and erythroderma to protect the skin barrier
Monitor baseline tryptase and assess for systemic involvement, taking precautions around intercurrent illness and procedures
Refer to specialist dermatology and paediatric mastocytosis services and premedicate before procedures and anaesthesia
